rows.question: How is committees of National Biodiversity Authority defined for the purposes of the Biological Diversity Act, 2002?
rows.asked_question: How is committees of National Biodiversity Authority defined for the purposes of the Biological Diversity Act, 2002?
rows.answer_text: The National Biodiversity Authority may constitute a committee to deal with agro‑biodiversity and may also constitute any number of committees it deems fit for the efficient discharge of its duties and performance of its functions under the Act[1]. Such committees may co‑opt persons who are not members of the Authority to attend meetings and take part in proceedings, although those co‑opted persons do not have the right to vote[1].

rows.question: What are the consequences of cognizance of offences?
rows.asked_question: What are the consequences of cognizance of offences?
rows.answer_text: A court may not take cognizance of an offence under the Biodiversity Act, Trade Marks Act or Geographical Indications Act unless a written complaint is filed by the Central Government, the Registrar or an authorised officer, meaning proceedings cannot be initiated without such a complaint [1][2][3]. Certain offences listed in those statutes are designated as cognizable, permitting police officers of at least deputy superintendent rank to conduct warrant‑less searches and seizures and to produce the seized items before a Metropolitan or Judicial Magistrate of the first class [2][3]. Courts inferior to a Metropolitan Magistrate or Judicial Magistrate of the first class are barred from trying those offences, limiting trial jurisdiction to higher courts [2][3].

cited_evidence.citation: Geographical Indications of Goods (Registration and Protection) Act, 1999 — Section 50
